author: Alfred the Great's Circle / Anonymous

sentences.translation: Ohthere said to his lord, King Alfred, that he lived the furthest north of all Norwegians.
He said that he lived in the northern part of the land by the West Sea (ocean west of Norway).

He said though that the land continues very long to the north from there, but it is all uninhabited, except in a few places here and there Finns (i.e. Sami) camp, hunting in winter and in summer fishing by the sea.
He said that on one occasion he wanted to find out how far that land lay to the north, or whether anyone lived to the north of the wilderness.
Then he traveled north near the land.
The whole way he kept the empty land to his starboard and the open sea to his port side for three days; then he was as far north as the whale hunters travel at the farthest.
Then he traveled still northwards as far as he could sail in the next three days.

Then the land turned eastwards, or the sea turned into the land, he did not know which, but he knew that he waited there for wind from the west and a little from the north and then sailed east by land as far as he could sail in four days.
Then he had to wait there for a wind from due north, because the land turned south there, or the sea turned into the land, he did not know which.
Then he sailed southwards from there near land as far as he could sail in five days.
There a large river led up into the land.
Then they turned up into the river, because they did not dare sail forth by the river for fear of hostility, because the land was all settled on the other side of the river.

He had not encountered any settled land before since he traveled from his own home, but the whole way there there had been empty land to his starboard except for fishermen and fowlers and hunters, and they were all Finns, and open sea was always to his port side.
The Bjarmians (Permians?, Komi?) had very widely cultivated their land, but they (Ohthere and his crew) did not dare go there.
But the land of the Terfinns (Ter-Sami?) was all uninhabited, except where hunters camped, or fishermen or fowlers.
Many stories the Bjarmians told him both about their own land and about the lands that were around them, but he did not know how much was true, because he did not see it himself.
The Finns, it seemed to him, and the Bjarmians spoke almost the same language.

He traveled there mostly, in addition to the exploration of the land, for the walruses, because they have very fine bone in their teeth (the teeth they brought some of for the king), and their hide is very good for ships' ropes.
This whale is much smaller than other whales: it is not longer than 7 ells ($sim$14 feet) long.
But in his own land is the best whale hunting: those (whales) are 48 ells long and the biggest 50 ells long.
Of these (whales), he said that he as part of a crew of 6 (whalers) killed 60 in two days.
He was a very wealthy man in the possessions that their wealth is based on, which is wild beasts.
He still had, when he visited the king, 600 unsold tame animals.
Those animals they call reindeer; of these, 6 were decoy reindeer, which are very valuable to the Finns, because they catch the wild reindeer with them.
He was among the principal men in that land, though he did not have more than 20 cows and 20 sheep and 20 swine, and the little (land) that he ploughed, he ploughed with horses.
But their income is mostly from the tribute that the Finns pay to them.
The tribute consists of animal skins and bird feathers and whale bone and the ships' ropes that are made from whale and seal hides.
Each pays according to his rank.

The highest ranking have to pay 15 marten skins and 5 reindeer skins and 1 bear skin and 10 ambers (unit of measurement) of feathers and a bear-skin or otter-skin coat and 2 ships' ropes; each is 60 ells long: one is made from whale skin, and the other from seal skin.
He said that the Norwegians' land is very long and very narrow.
All that one can either graze or plow of it, that lies by the sea, and even that is very rocky in some places.
And wild moors lie to the east and above, along the settled land; in the moors live Finns.
And the settled land is widest to the east and the further north (one goes) the narrower (it becomes).
Eastward it can be 60 miles wide, or a little wider, and in the middle it can be 30 (miles) or wider.

And northward, he said, where it is narrowest, that it could be three miles wide to the moor, and the moor afterwards is as wide in some places as one can travel over in two weeks, and in some places as wide as one can travel over in six days.
Then along the southern part of the land (Norway), on the other side of the moor, is Sweden, until the northern part of the land; and along the northern part of the land is Cwen (Kven) land.
The Cwens sometimes raid the Norwegians across the moor, sometimes the Norwegians raid them.
And there are very large freshwater lakes throughout the moors, and the Cwens carry their ships over land to the lakes and from there raid the Norwegians; they have very small and very light ships.
Ohthere said that the district that he lived in is called Hålogaland.
He said that no one lived to the north of him.
Then in the south of the land is a port that one calls Skiringssal.
He said that one could not sail there in one month if they camped at night and had favorable wind every day.
And all the while he must sail by land.
And to his starboard first there is Ireland and then the islands that are between Ireland (Shetlands, Orkneys, Hebrides?) and this land (Britain).

sentences.translation: Then there is this land (to the starboard) until he comes to Skiringssal, and the whole way to the port side is Norway.

South of Skiringssal a very large sea leads up into the land; it is wider than anyone can see over, and Jutland is opposite on the other side and then Sillende (an area of the Jutland peninsula south of what is being called Jutland here).
The sea runs many hundred miles up into the land.

And from Skiringssal he said that he sailed in five days to the port that one calls Hedeby; it stands between the Wends (i.e. Slavs) and the Saxons and Angeln (the peninsula), and it belongs to the Danes.

When he was sailing there from Skiringssal, on his port side was Denmark (now Halland and Skåne in Sweden), and on his starboard was open sea for three days; and then, for two days before he came to Hedeby, on his starboard were Jutland and Sillende and many islands.
In those lands lived the English, before they came here to (this) land.
And to his port side for those two days were the islands that belong to Denmark.
Wulfstan said that he traveled from Hedeby, that he was in Truso in seven days and nights, that the ship was the whole way running under sail.
Wendland was to his starboard, and to his port side were Langeland and Lolland and Falster and Skåne; and these lands all belong to Denmark.
And then Burgundy (Bornholm) was to the port side, and they have their own king.
Then after Burgundy, to our port side were these lands that are called first Blekinge island, and (then) Möre and Öland and Gotland; and these lands begong to the Swedes.
And Wendland was to our starboard the whole way until the mouth of the Vistula.
The Vistula is a very large river, and it separates Witland and Wendland, and that Witland belongs to the Ests.
And the Vistula leads out of Wendland and leads into the Est Sea (Vistula Lagoon), and the Est Sea is at least 15 miles wide.

Then the Elbląg (river) comes from the east into the Est Sea from the lake where Truso stands on the shore, and the Elbląg from the east from Estland and the Vistula from the south from Wendland come out together into the Est Sea, and then the Elbląg deprives the Vistula of its name (i.e. takes the name of the Vistula), and (the combined river) leads from the lake west and north to sea; therefore one calls it the mouth of the Vistula.
That Estland is very large, and there are very many towns, and in each town is a king.
And there is very much honey and fishing; and the king and the richest men drink mare's milk, and the non-wealthy and the servants drink mead.
There is much conflict between them.
And there isn't any ale brewed among the Ests, but there is sufficient mead.

And there is a custom with the Ests that when a man dies, he lies inside inside uncremated with his kinsmen and friends for a month, and sometimes two, and the kings and the other high-ranking men, so much longer as they have more wealth, sometimes half a year that they will remain uncremated; and lie above ground in their houses.
And all the while that the body is inside, there must be be drinking and playing, until the day that they cremate him.

Then the same day that they wish to carry him to the (funeral) pyre, they divide apart his property that remains there after the drinking and the playing into five or six (parts), sometimes into more, as the amount of the property may be.

Then they lay out the largest part of it about one mile from the town, then the second, then the third, until it is all laid within that one mile, and the smallest part shall be nearest to the town that the dead man lived in.
Then all the men that have the swiftest horses in the land shall be assembled, about five or six miles from the property.

Then they all run towards the property; then the man who has the swiftest hors comes to the first and the largest part, and so each after the other, until it is all taken, and he who takes the smallest part is he who runs for the property nearest to the town.
And then each rides on his way with the property, and can have it all; and therefore swift horses are immensely valuable there.
And when his property is thus all spent, then one carries him out and cremates (him) with his weapons and clothing.
And most (commonly) they spend away all his wealth with the long lying of the dead man inside, and what they lay out on the roads, which the strangers run to and take (away).
And it is a custom with the Ests that there men of every tribe must be cremated; and if there one finds a single bone uncremated, they must atone for it greatly.
And there is among the Ests a power such that they can make coldness; and therefore the dead men lie there so long and do not decay, because they work the cold onto him.

sentences.translation: And if one sets out two vessels full of ale or water, they make it such that either will be frozen over, whether it be summer or winter.
